utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-95-13/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Mile Mrksic, Miroslav Radic, and Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. I'll start with you, Mr. Mrksic. Good afternoon to you. THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, good afternoon to you too, and the same question: Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes, I can follow it in the language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a chair. Mr. Radic, good afternoon to you too. Can you follow the proceedings in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow the proceedings, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, my name is Jan Wubben, senior trial attorney. Included in the Prosecution team also are my co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Kristina Carey, Ms. Joanne Richardson, together with Diane Boles, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you all. Appearances for Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. The Defence of Mr. Mrksic will be represented by attorney Mr. Vasic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, to you. Appearance for the accused Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Novak Lukic, I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon to you. And appearances for Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I'm Borivoje Borovic, attorney-at-law, and together is my colleague Mira Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you all. You are -- you are aware that there are two things happening this afternoon. One is a Status Conference, and that will come later on in the day. We will start with the further appearance of accused Radic and Sljivancanin. Now, my suggestion is as follows, that instead of having Mr. Mrksic walk out and then walk in, he will stay here in the courtroom unless he prefers himself not to be here. But there is also another understanding; that since this is, strictly speaking, none of his business, it may well be that, for example, Mr. Sljivancanin does -- would rather prefer that he pleads or makes a statement with regard to the amended indictment, consolidated indictment, not in the presence of either of the two -- either or both of the two other accused. The same applies to Mr. Radic. He may prefer to make his statement or enter his plea not in the presence of accused Sljivancanin and accused Mrksic. That's an option which I'm leaving open. If any one of you appears not to have, Mr. Sljivancanin, while I am dealing only with you and not with Mr. Mrksic, then you only have to draw my attention to that and Mr. Mrksic will be out of the courtroom and then will come back for the Status Conference. Did I make myself clear? All right. So we are going to start with the further appearance of Mr. Radic and Mr. Sljivancanin, but before I do so, I think I ought to express my gratitude in public to both the Prosecution, Mr. Wubben, and to the members of the Defence -- various Defence teams for your cooperation in enabling me to shift the initial -- the further appearance and the Status Conference from earlier on this afternoon for which time it was scheduled to now. Unfortunately, due to a change in the time schedule under which I was dealing with another case, we did not become aware that there would be a clash with the hearing of this afternoon, and that would have created some problems. They could have been solved, but this is the best solution of all, and I am thanking you publicly for your cooperation. These things will not go unnoticed, neither now nor later on. And I shall go straight to the merits of the further appearance and point out for your benefit but also for the benefit of the public and those who are following these proceedings that pursuant to the Trial Chamber's collegial decision on form of consolidated amended indictment, and on the Prosecution's application to amend the indictment of the 23rd of January of 2004, the Prosecution subsequently filed the 9 February 2004 consolidated amended indictment. This 9 February 2004 consolidated amended indictment contains four new charges against Mr. Radic and against Mr. Sljivancanin respectively. These four new charges are persecution, extermination, and torture, the latter being charged both as a crime against humanity and as a violation of the laws and customs of war. Rule 50(B) of this Tribunal establishes that if the amended indictment includes new charges and the accused has already appeared before a Trial Chamber in accordance with Rule 62, then a further appearance shall be held as soon as practicable to enable the accused to enter a plea on the new charges. You are also aware of the other accused's right when new charges are added to an already existing indictment as far as -- in other words, his right in particular to seek an adjournment before -- or to enable him or her, as it may be the case, to enter a plea. I understand that in the course of the contacts that have been made, particularly the Rule 65 ter meeting of this morning, there is no indication that either of the two accused, that is Sljivancanin and Radic, want an adjournment. Am I right in that? I see Mr. Borivoje Borovic nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. We will not ask for any adjournment; we can plead today to the amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I also noticed Mr. Lukic nodding too for Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can also confirm, Your Honour, that we will ask for no adjournment, and our client will plead today to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Our Rules also -- I thank you both for your practical approach to this matter and for your cooperation. You are also aware that in terms of our Rules, once an indictment is amended, there is always the right of the accused to have that indictment read out in its entirety in public. Of course, the Trial Chamber is prepared to do that if there is an indication in that direction from either of the two accused, but I have been given to understand that in the course of the 65 ter meeting that was held under the Chairmanship of my senior legal officer, Mr. Von Hebel, there was agreement with the two Defence teams for Mr. Radic and Mr. Sljivancanin that there is no need for the Trial Chamber, for me as the Pre-Trial Judge in this -- in this case, to read out the entire amended indictment, the so-called 9 February 2004 consolidated amended indictment, and that it will be sufficient if I read out only to the accused the gist of the added charges. Do you agree that this is the case and this is what will happen? Again, Mr. Radic -- sorry, Mr. Lukic or -- yes, Mr. Borovic. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We had only a brief time to spend with our client before we entered the courtroom. We talked about the amended indictment. The client has comprehended the amendments, so there is no need to read and go through them, we have already completed that part of the work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Borovic, and I also thank your client for his cooperation. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Sljivancanin, in a brief conversation, also allowed -- told me that there is no need to read the entire indictment. He has knowledge of the indictment, and he will simply plead to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I once more thank you, Mr. Lukic, as well, and I also thank you, Mr. Sljivancanin, for your cooperation. Now, I am going to concentrate on you, Mr. Radic, and I want to make sure that you have received the 9 February 2004 consolidated amended indictment in your own language. Is that correct? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is correct. I have understood everything that is stated in the indictment by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question, did you understand its contents, but you have already told me that you did. THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Entirely, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also want to make it clear that -- I don't know if you have noticed it or not, certainly your lawyer, your Defence counsel has, but the numbering and the order of the counts has been altered vis-a-vis the previous indictment, and that's because of the general exercise that was done in consolidating the three indictments. I have already indicated that there seems to be an agreement, and I got a confirmation of this to read out only to you the new charges contained in the 9 February 2004 consolidated amended indictment. This is precisely what I'm going to do now. As I go through each of these counts, I will be asking you if you want to plead, enter a plea, to that particular count and what kind of a plea you would like to enter. Take your time. This is a matter of great responsibility for every accused. I realise that you have waived your right to have an adjournment on this matter. If you need any time to think about it, let me know and I will give you all the time in the world in terms and within the limits laid down by our Statute and by our Rules and Regulations. Did I make myself clear to you? Okay. THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Radic, the first count against you is a charge of persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, this being a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(h) and Article 7(1) as well as Article 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal. Are you aware of this? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to enter a plea to this charge? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you plead; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, Madam Registrar, accused Radic has pleaded not guilty to the first count, that is the one of persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds. I now move to the second count. The second count against you is one of extermination, this being also a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(b) and Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of our Statute, that is the Statute of this Tribunal. Do you want to enter a plea? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what is your plea? Do you plead guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, Madam Registrar, the accused Radic has pleaded not guilty to the second count that -- this being one of extermination. The fifth count. Now, the fifth count against you is one of torture, a crime against humanity, punishable under 5(f), Article 5(f) and again Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal. I take it that you are in a position to enter a plea, and I will move straight away to asking you whether you plead guilty or not guilty to this charge. THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Radic. Madam Registrar, for the record, Mr. Radic has entered a plea of not guilty to the fifth count, this being a charge of torture as being a crime against humanity. Then there is the seventh count against you, Mr. Radic, and this is again once more a charge of torture, but this time you're being charged with torture as being a -- in violation of the laws or customs of war as recognised by Common Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Article 3, and Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal. How do you plead to this seventh count? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Madam Registrar, for the record, Mr. Radic has entered a plea of not guilty with regard to the seventh count. So, Mr. Radic, please sit down. Thank you. And again I want to make sure, Madam Registrar, that you have noted that Mr. Radic has pleaded not guilty to counts 1, 2, 5, and 7 of the 9 February 2004 consolidated amended indictment. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Colonel Sljivancanin. This is more or less going to be a repetition of the same procedure, and so I want to make sure first and foremost that you have received the indictment in your own language or in a language that you understand. When I say "the indictment," it's the 9 February 2004 consolidated amended indictment. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] I have received it, I read it, and I understood its content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So I skip the second question, which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was precisely did you understand its contents. I am also making you aware, just as I did with Mr. Radic, that the sequence, the number and the order of the various charges in the consolidated amended indictment has changed, but I am sure that you are aware of this. If not, I will explain to you how the sequence -- how the order of the various counts has changed. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] I have talked to my Defence counsel, and he has informed me about that. We spoke for some half an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So now I'm going to follow the same procedure. I am going to read out to you, count by count, the new added charges against you, and then I will ask you how you would like to plea. If you are not prepared to plea today, please make that known to me, and we will protect your rights and will give you enough time to think about it, and then you will enter your plea later on. The first count against you in terms of the 9 February 2004 consolidated amended indictment is one of persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, this being a crime against humanity, which is punishable under Article 5(h) and Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal. How do you plead to this first count of persecution; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sljivancanin, and that goes on the record, Madam Registrar. The second count against you is one of extermination, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(b) and Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal. How do you plead to this charge? THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sljivancanin. The fifth count against you is one of torture, this being a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(f) and Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you plead to this added count; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Not guilty to this count as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sljivancanin. And the seventh count against you is again one of torture, however this time it's being charged as a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Common Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Article 3 and Article 7(1) and 7(3) of our Statute. How do you plead to this count; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down, Colonel Sljivancanin. And I want to make sure that Madam Registrar has noted down for the record that Mr. Sljivancanin has pleaded not guilty to counts 1, 2, 5, and 7 of the 9 February 2004 consolidated amended indictment. You could have chosen a shorter title. I have to repeat this every time. We are now going to convert ourselves into a Status Conference. The further appearance of Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Radic is over unless there is anything you would like to draw my attention to. There is none. So we are now going to give a start to the Status Conference. Again, for the record, I wish to remind everyone that the last Status Conference for the three accused, Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin, was held way back on the 22nd of October of 2003. Under Rule 65 bis of our Rules and Regulations, the Trial Chamber is required to hold a Status Conference within 120 days after the previous Status Conference, after the last Status Conference, and this is being precisely held within that time limit laid down or provided for in our Rules. The purpose of the Status Conference, of the periodical Status Conferences, is twofold mainly; the first being to organise exchanges between the parties with a view to ensuring an expeditious preparation for trial. The second is to give an opportunity to the accused to raise any issue related to the mental and physical condition. That includes also the conditions of detention, as per the practice of this Tribunal. I wish also to state here, again this is for public consumption and not because I would imagine that you have forgotten what happened this morning, that in preparation for this Status Conference a meeting pursuant to Rule 65 ter was held between the parties and the senior -- the representatives of the parties of the accused and my Senior Legal Officer today at 9.30, which I understand was very constructive and very fruitful, and I wish to thank you both Prosecution and the three Defence teams for your cooperation. The issues raised therein which do not require a decision from the Pre-Trial Judge need not be raised again during this Status Conference unless you have reason not -- you have reason to disagree. In other words, you will have every opportunity to raise again some issues that were debated there which need not be decided if you feel there is the need, but otherwise, please refrain from raising the same matters again. And I start with outstanding motions. I start with you, Mr. Mrksic. I start with you. You needn't stand up. You may remain seated. As far as I am aware, there is a Defence motion for review of the Registrar's decision of the 25th of September, 2002, filed by your lawyers, denying payment of expenses related to pre-trial investigative work. Now, this is an old story, you remember, and it had already started when Mr. Sljivancanin, Mr. Radic, had not yet arrived here in The Hague. We had put it in the deep freeze for some time, but it has been warmed up, resurrected, and we will soon be handing down our decision. It has been more or less prepared, and it's in the process of cooking, and as soon as it is ready, we will let you have it. It should not take a long time. We have worked on it, we have taken into account every single document and the details of the documents that we received, and we should be able to hand down the decision pretty soon. But that's not a decision that I will take myself, it's a combined effort of the three Judges forming -- constituting Trial Chamber II. In other words, the other two Judges have to come back to me and we need to discuss maybe a little bit further. There is another motion on -- filed by you or on your behalf, Mr. Mrksic, and that is what I would rather call Defence request in - my country we would say humble request - on the level of the case which has been assigned by the Registrar. Here, I must confess, we have not yet reached an advanced stage in our deliberations, but it will receive its utmost attention. As soon as we are ready with the other motion, we will move to deal with this one. With regard to these two motions, Mr. Vasic, do you have anything to state?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for the information you have provided us with. We expect our two motions to receive a decision because they will affect our ability for defending our client, and we hope that it will be along the lines of what you said today and according to those guidelines. So I thank you for that. A decision is vital in view of the work we have to do, and as I expound in my motion, this will inquire -- require additional expenses, and so we will need to get the monies we have asked for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I am not addressing you, Mr. Wubben, because I think this is at the moment more of the accused's concern rather than yours. You will only be interested in reading the decision at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. We don't take a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I'm not asking for submissions, I'm just asking for comments on what I stated. Then, Mr. Vasic, on the 17th of October of last year, you filed an additional request for a review of the Registrar's decision granting additional allotment of 350 working hours at the counsel rate and 1.500 hours -- 15.000 hours, I may stand corrected here, the supporting staff rate to your Defence team. You requested -- or you prayed this Trial Chamber to review the Registrar's decision and you qualify the case of Mile Mrksic at that level of complexity. This is precisely the motion I referred to regarding the level of the case. Before we conclude on this matter, I wanted to make sure, has there been any further contacts between you and the Registrar with regard to the level of the case and the number of hours and rates fixed by the -- by the Registrar? And I'm asking you because later on, I told you already, that we would have started dealing with this as soon as we would have disposed of the previous motion. But one of the things I would have certainly asked is whether there has been any discussions or negotiations since the 17th of October between you and the Registrar on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should like to inform you that the Defence did request categorisation for this trial, and the Registrar has not made a decision, but it has given us the allotment of hours that you yourself mentioned. So this number of hours is not in conformity with the categorisation of the case itself, and we consider as the case stands now would merit category 2, and we think that the Vukovar case, a case which refers to Vukovar, cannot be deemed to be the simplest of cases, especially in view of the media exploitation of that case and by the Prosecution in the bygone period. I apologise, yes? So I consider that the Registrar should have made a decision to class the case into group 2 and not to allot a lesser number of hours than we would otherwise receive. This is a very important matter because we need to do a lot of work, and I set it out, the work we need to do, in my request and motion. Having received an answer from the Registrar and having contacted the Trial Chamber, I had no further contacts with the Registrar. I did not initiate such contacts, nor did the Registrar for his part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure of that, because if there have been further negotiations following the filing of that motion, then I want to make it clear that we ought to be put into the picture, even if they are still pending. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Vasic. According to my records, these are the only two outstanding matters, outstanding motions that your client has. Are you aware of anything else beyond that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour. Those were the only two requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Borovic, I'm now going to address your client's outstanding motions according to my records; and according to my records he has only got one outstanding motion, that is the one filed on the 27th of October of last year relating to the Registrar's decision of 20 days earlier, of the 7th October. On the 27th October, you filed a request to the Trial Chamber praying that we review the Registrar's decision which I mentioned to you, which, inter alia, states that the accused should bear the costs associated with 223 hours of investigative and legal assistance work at the pre-trial stage. You also requested the Trial Chamber to rule that the cost of 223 hours of investigative work at the pre-trial stage be borne by the Tribunal. I suppose -- am I going too fast for the interpreters? A bit. A bit. So I will try to slow down. You are definitely aware that by order of the Trial Chamber, the Registry, or the Registrar, filed comments and associated material on the 12th of January of this year. The Registrar is requesting the Trial Chamber to deny your client's motion and confirm the Registrar's decision on partial indigence of the accused. We gave you an opportunity to respond to this, and you responded on the 26th of January of 2004, requesting the Trial Chamber to quash the Registrar's decision. Now, this is still pending, and to be honest with you, we worked first on Mr. Mrksic's motion where we thought of establishing one or more principles that should regulate the matter, and then we will eventually follow up with a decision in your client's case. Do you wish to state anything in this regard? Not further submissions, just remarks on what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, we have made our request and we have provided a comment and response to the one made by the Registrar, but my colleague, Mrs. Mira Tapuskovic, will give you additional information.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We did not wish to abuse your time when you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have all the time --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't thinking during this particular Status Conference, but thank you for that anyway. But in writing our comments and responding to the comments of the Registrar and following your guidelines contained in the decision, we did try to adhere strictly to the instructions that were given and to provide you with the answers that you asked for. As you have just noted yourself, Your Honour, it was the intention of the Trial Chamber to deal with Mrksic's request first, and as we can say, there are two Mrksic requests that are pending. We consider that at this point in time there is nothing for us to add to the request already made but that it should take its course, and the Trial Chamber will pay sufficient care and attention and time to the response by the Registrar and our own comments as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Tapuskovic. As I said, this will be dealt with in due course. As you are aware, each case has its own characteristics. There are principles of law and procedure that are applicable to the three accused, but then of course what will be the outcome of each and every application, motion, very much depends on everything that one needs to throw in the basket when we start making our deliberations. Am I correct, Mr. Borovic, in stating that there are no further motions pending from your client, or do you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You're quite right; no further motions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Colonel Sljivancanin, until yesterday or until early this morning, there was nothing pending from you, no outstanding motions, but there is one now, I understand. Mr. Lukic, could you just describe to the Trial Chamber what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll just briefly tell you what it is about. So far I have followed the correspondence between the Registrar and Mr. Radic's Defence with respect to the number of hours allotted by the Registrar or, rather, the Registrar has said that it will not finance this number of hours for the Radic Defence. And also we looked at the appointment for permanent Defence counsels, I myself and Mr. Bulatovic as the co-counsel, and the Registrar in that respect made a similar decision with respect to the expenses involving Mr. Sljivancanin. The Registrar found that there were certain material resources, if I can use that term, which would be able to cover part of the Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin. In my opinion, this is a position of principle on the part of the Registrar with -- and his approach to the material resources and property of the family of the accused, and it is a matter of principle on the part of the Defence team, and it is similar to the correspondence I saw in Mr. Radic's case with respect to the material resources of the family and their possibility to finance part of the Defence for the accused. So that was the reason why we filed our motion and made our request based on a similar principle as was resorted to by the Radic Defence. And I'm sure this Trial Chamber will once again find itself having to make a decision which will cover both, that is to say the Registrar's attitude and their duty to pay for the Defence counsels of the accused. So that is basically what our request entails. And we have also attended correspondence between the Registrar and ourselves and the Registrar and Mr. Radic. Of course, the situation is specific in the case of Mr. Sljivancanin's family, and we set that out in our own motion, and that is the substance of our own request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. As you can imagine, I have not had a copy of your motion made available. I will go through it adequately as soon as it is forwarded to me, and I will deal with it accordingly. But again, this matter will receive all the adequate attention, and again may I point out that each case is different, has its own characteristics, and we are precisely dealing not just with principles but also matters over which the Registrar seems to have quite a discretion. And there are no other motions pending from Colonel Sljivancanin? That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. There are no other motions at this stage from Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. And talking of motions, I am going to mention something which is of paramount importance because it also involves deadlines, making it clear that I'm not prepared to go beyond deadlines once they are stipulated by the Rules and Regulations. Now, the first statement that I want to make refers to all the three accused, and you have no later than the 8th March of this year to file preliminary motions pursuant to Rule 72 in respect of the new aspects that emerge out of the 9 February 2004 consolidated amended indictment. Please stick to this deadline. Don't come to me one day late, because your request will not be entertained unless there is serious justification. Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Miroslav Radic received the indictment on the 12th of February, and the Registrar submitted it on the 6th of February, that is to say with a six-day delay, and those six days would have meant a great deal to us. So that by Court decision we could get 30 days for our motion to this consolidated amended indictment. So that would be our request, because we have received very extensive material that we have to study along with the document itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vasic and Mr. Lukic, do you want to join in Mr. Borovic's request?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listening to Mr. Borovic, the Defence teams did indeed receive the indictment with a six-day delay, along with a lot of supporting material which the OTP provided us following instructions from the Trial Chamber, and this supporting material, as far as I can see, amounts to about 250 pages, and perhaps my colleague Mr. Borovic's request is justified in view of the fact that we have to study all that material to see whether there is any scope for any motions, preliminary motions pursuant to Rule 82. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I join in the proposal made by Mr. Borovic in full, and let me tell you that I received the indictment on the 11th of February, one day before him, but that doesn't change matters. This is the supporting material that I'm holding in my hand now, the bulk of it, and which I have to look through with my client first of all. So you must bear in mind the fact that we're not always in The Hague. So we have to look through the material with our clients and then receive instructions from our clients with respect to writing motions or anything like that. So we think that five or six additional days would mean a great deal to us and I don't think it would be a hindrance to the other side in the proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, do you have any objection at all that the time limit be extended from the 8th March to the 12th March?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There was indeed a kind of delay so the argumentation of this limited time of extension is reasonable. I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does anybody have a calendar here, because I was not expecting this, obviously, and I want to know what day of the week is the 12th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would that be agreeable to you? Yes. I see the three counsel nodding. So I go back to what I stated earlier. The time limit which you will have for the filing of preliminary motions pursuant to Rule 72 will expire on the 8th -- on the 12th of March, 2004, there being no objection on the part of the Prosecutor. And I wish to thank you, Mr. Wubben, on behalf of the Prosecutor, for accepting this and showing again cooperation with this Trial Chamber. And we move to disclosures, and we have various kinds of disclosures to deal with. I will deal first with disclosures under Rule 66(A)(i). And I am informed that counsel for the accused have, the three of them, agreed that this material has been disclosed to each one of them. This actually is in confirmation of what was stated during the previous status conference. I take it that the situation has not changed and that, therefore, all disclosures under this Rule 66(A)(i) have been carried out. Correct? And then we have a slightly more complicated matter which I hope will not require the intervention of myself as Pre-Trial Judge or of the Trial Chamber. We're talking of Rule 66(A)(ii) statements. There is a partially confidential Prosecution's first report concerning disclosure which was filed on the 1st of August, 2003, in which -- or by means of which the Trial Chamber was -- received confidential attachment A, namely the materials disclosed to Defence counsel for Mrksic and Radic and to also Colonel Sljivancanin at the time he was unrepresented, you will remember, pursuant to the Rule I mentioned earlier. That's 66(A)(ii). I am informed by my staff who were present for the 65 ter meeting that the Prosecution, it seems, has since then assured counsel for Colonel Sljivancanin that the material which he received from his client was the same that had been disclosed pursuant to Rules 66 and 68 to counsel of the other two accused. Is that correct, Mr. Borovic -- Mr. Lukic? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, at the last Status Conference - that is October of last year - Mr. Wubben, you had stated or announced that the Prosecution would continue its disclosure of these statements, that is under Rule 66(A)(ii), at the pace of the searches carried out by its evidence unit. How far have we proceeded along this path?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Kristina Carey will give you additional information, but I might start with the conference this morning, 65 ter conference, at which Mr. Vasic underlined that so far only a number of five statements had been given. We couldn't check that during the Status Conference, but afterwards we checked this out and Ms. Kristina Carey will further inform you of the status of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Carey, please. Thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this point the Prosecution is continuing. The combination of what we have turned over in, I believe, three different batches of supporting materials in addition to what we sent in the July package, we have turned over the ICTY statements and as much material as could be searched from the database on our own behalf or from prior trials of 23 witnesses comprised of our still ongoing witness list. It is anticipated that we will ultimately have a witness list that is approximately between 60 and 80 witnesses, so that constitutes somewhere between a third and a quarter of our total possible witnesses. We are, as we discussed in the 65 ter conference, have still, despite our efforts, not been prioritised with the Internet search unit, but we are undertaking at this point, as we have assured counsel, that we are going to at least deal quickly with the issue of turning over ICTY statements and of course dealing with any issues of protection from prior Trial Chambers and any protective measures that our witnesses may request. So that is the progress that we have made to date, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Carey. Do you have any comments? Starting with Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Today during our 65 ter conference, we discussed this matter at length with our learned friends. The Defence gave its position, namely that the disclosure under this Rule is very important for timely preparation of the Defence before the beginning of the trial. I have a lot of understanding for the problems encountered by my learned friends. There was even some discussion of aiding them by giving them a certain deadline to disclose this material, which would again update the requests regarding the OTP. However, my learned friends said that they will believe they would be able to abide by the deadlines on their own and that that would further facilitate the disclosure under this Rule 66. The Defence is grateful to our learned friends from the OTP, and if there should be any need, we would ask for your assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that there are two minor problems. The first one is with respect to Rule 66(A)(ii). We received a small number of statements concerning the issues we have here in this trial. The witness statements we received will not be of much assistance to us in preparing our defence. The 60 to 80 witnesses which the OTP intends to call to testify, apparently only a small number would be brought here to testify, which means that they did not want to burden the Defence with all that material. We think, with all due respect to the OTP, that it is in their ability to do a little bit more to assist Defence in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Thank you, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not want to repeat what I said at the 65 ter conference, but what I think is of vital importance here is to enable the Defence to prepare itself in a timely manner for the trial. What concerns me is that we can face the possible beginning of the trial in a situation where all the teams are overburdened with work, writing their pre-trial briefs, scheduling Pre-Trial Conferences, and so on, and so that we, Defence counsel who have only two-member teams, unlike the OTP, we must be able to timely and efficiently prepare for the trial. If we should receive material shortly before the trial begins, we will have no equality of arms in the trial; we will not be able to prepare ourselves adequately for all witnesses. The task of the OTP is to, of course, prepare their witnesses and then inform the Defence about their witnesses. Should we fail to receive that material in a timely manner, then we will not be able to do our job. The OTP told us that they do not want to burden us with statements of witnesses which might not come here to testify, whereas we believe that it would be important for us to receive everything so that we can make an assessment ourselves and see what we need to do in order to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Mr. Lukic. The position as I see it is that, for the time being, as I see it, I have no reason to entertain any doubts that the present situation is in any way prejudicial to any of the three accused. I can assure you that this Trial Chamber will leave no stone unturned in ensuring that there is no disparity between the Prosecution and the Defence when it comes to exact resources because the resources are always different with regard to arms, as some of us prefer to refer to it. I think the best way to do is to exhort you, Mr. Wubben, to accelerate this process of disclosure under 66(A)(ii). Accelerate it as much as possible. And I will leave it to the next Status Conference, when we will still be pretty far from the date of the trial, to make an assessment of the situation as it will obtain then, and if it is necessary at that point in time for the Trial Chamber to fix a time limit within which to carry out this obligation under Rule 66(A)(ii), then we will -- we will not hesitate to do it. That might also not be the case, as experience in other cases has taught me. I mean, sometimes it's not always that possible for the Prosecution to abide by -- by this rule to the letter at the pre-trial stage or at the early stages of the pre-trial stage, and I'm sure that you are also well experienced to know exactly what I mean. But I will be keeping a watchful eye, I or the Judge who will succeed me as Pre-Trial Judge in this case, and that will, of course, be a subject matter that will certainly come up in the next agenda for the next Status Conference which will be held according to the Rules. Yes. Now I come to disclosure under Rule 68, which as you know has been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the subject of an amendment by the Plenary, effective 24th December of last year. I'm referring to the Prosecution's obligation to disclose exculpatory and other relevant material. Just for the benefit of the public who is perhaps not aware as we certainly are of the nature of the amendment to this Rule, I just -- will just give a very brief explanation. The amended Rule 68 provides, inter alia, that the Prosecution shall, as soon as practicable, disclose to the Defence any material which in the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor may suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence. And secondly, the Prosecution shall make available to the Defence in electronic form collections of relevant material held by it together with appropriate computer software with which the Defence can search such collections electronically. I will be asking the three of you for your comments, as well as you, Mr. Wubben, your remarks on this particular procedure. What I can state here is what I know, and that refers to the partially confidential Prosecution first report concerning disclosure, which was filed last year on the 1st of August just before we broke for the summer recess; and then the Prosecution's second report concerning disclosure filed practically a month later, on the 4th of September, 2003; and again the partially confidential Prosecution third report concerning disclosure which is dated 21st of October, 2003, which taken together detail the material disclosed pursuant to Rule 68 to the three accused. That was the position as it obtained under the old Rule. Has the new Rule changed anything? So I would start with you, Mr. Wubben. Is there any other material under Rule 68, as amended, that you need to disclose?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will request Ms. Kristina Carey to give you additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Carey.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: At this point my understanding is that the Defence counsel has in the interim been made available in electronic form a substantial number of documents, the exact number of which I am not certain of, by the OTP in a searchable, I believe computer form, either -- I believe they have the computer system and searching application, and I understand that that will continue to be updated. At this point, we do not -- we do not have -- we will continue with our obligation to disclose any materials that come to our -- to our attention in the course of our work and make those available as we find them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vasic, do you have any comments on this matter and also on the Prosecutor's statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You have probably been informed about our discussions on this matter during 65 ter conference. The Defence believes that disclosure under Rule 68 could proceed faster and be more complete, especially because the change of rules indicates that the OTP is aware of all the facts that could lead to the acquittal of the -- of our client, of the accused, or mitigating his situation. The Defence can contribute little to this, but we believe that the main key is in the hands of the OTP when it comes to the application of this rule, because they have everything at their disposal. As for the e-mail communication, my friend from the OTP stated the situation correctly. Mrs. Tapuskovic also spoke about that, and I think that she can do it now in this Status Conference like she did it this morning so that I do not cover the same topic as she will.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Vasic. I would like to inform my learned friends from the OTP -- to remind them, rather, that we received on three occasions material under Rule 68. That was on the 25th of July last year, on the 3rd of September last year, and during our last 65 ter conference in October of last year, and since then we have received nothing under that Rule. Following that, Rule 68 was changed in December of last year. All Defence teams working here at the Tribunal were informed about the possibility to carry out an electronic search of documents. I immediately found everything that our Defence team needed in order to have access to such documents. However, we immediately faced certain problems, namely that a large portion of the database is not accessible to us. We have been told that only 80 per cent of the database can be searched electronically, and the search process takes a long time, is not clear at all, and since all Defence teams, providing they fulfil certain criteria, have access to that database, that means that only material which is not confidential is available through the database, which means that that puts certain limitations on the Defence teams. However, since this is a new system which is still currently being developed here at the Tribunal, we will be flexible and patient in the hope that the system will be upgraded so that all the requirements of the Defence teams are met. We hope that we will be able to locate all of the material under Rule 68 using the electronic search mechanisms. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I enjoin you, Mr. Wubben, particularly to the complaints that Ms. Tapuskovic has raised about the adequacy of the system, to raise these matters with your superiors, because this tends to get fundamental in each and every case. On the other hand, Mr. Vasic, Mr. Borovic, Mr. Lukic, Ms. Tapuskovic, I do enjoin you to read carefully Rule 68. I appreciate your readiness to be patient. I strongly advise you to be patient, because I certainly wouldn't like to see Rule 68 being read and applied by the Prosecution as one way of loading you with all the material that they have laid their hands on irrespective of whether it's really material or not. I think one has to be practical and wise. Allow the Prosecution to take a considered decision as to what needs to be disclosed, particularly under the second part of Rule 68, because with regard to exculpatory material, I think that's pretty clear. But with regard to the rest, I would rather not have cabbages and Kings put together in one bag and try to see if I'm clever enough to distinguish one from the other, which sometimes it's easy, sometimes it's not, but it certainly will entail a lot - a lot - a lot of work. So the understanding is as follows: That this is an ongoing exercise. We ought to draw a distinction between exculpatory material proper, and the rest of the material that now the amended Rule 68 deals with, differently from what the situation was before. All right. I leave it entirely up to you, Mr. Wubben, and your team, of course, and you will report back to the Trial Chamber at the next Status Conference. Date for trial. Until a couple of months ago, I had hoped that this trial would be able to start relatively soon, but things have changed. We are giving it our utmost attention, but the estimate that we had that this trial will start around about the end of summer or beginning of summer of 2004 is no longer valid. What I can assure you of is that every effort will be made not to delay it unduly, but there are other cases that have matured and that were introduced before and have matured for trial, and obviously those take precedence unless there is serious reason to change the pattern which is applied by this Tribunal. Agreed facts. I'm not quite sure whether it's still early for me to enjoin the Defence teams and the Prosecution to sit down together and see if there are agreed facts to submit to the Trial Chamber in terms or pursuant to Rule 65 ter (H). If there are and you are in a position to start the exercise, please do so. If you prefer to wait and if you think it's more opportune to wait, then obviously I am in your hands and I am prepared to wait too, but don't do like several other lawyers in other cases, try to run away from this important provision that our Rules establish. It can be extremely useful, extremely economical, and I am pretty sure you realise that when there is such cooperation also in the course of the proceedings, the Trial Chamber never fails to take this or these similar matters in consideration however much important they may or however relevant they may be. Before we move to the final part of the Status Conference, are there any matters that either of the parties, any of the parties would like to raise? And then of course I will refer the same question to you, Mr. Wubben, but I was going to start with you straight away. Are there any matters you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic for accused Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no new matters to raise. I would simply like to thank you, Your Honour, for your timely response and understanding of the family circumstances of our client and enabling him to spend time with his family during this difficult time. Once again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, and understand that, and you have my condolences, as well as the Presiding Judge. Mr. Borovic, do you have any further matter to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would simply like to thank you for accepting to extend the deadline. I have no new matters to raise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No new matters. Thank you again for extending the deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you all. I turn now to Mr. Mrksic. You're familiar with this because this is how we end each and every Status Conference that we have. I am duty-bound under the Rules to inquire of you whether you wish to raise any matter which is related to your state of health or your condition of detention. Let's take state of health. Do you have any problems that you need to make the Trial Chamber aware of that in your considered opinion need our intervention? THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my health problems remain what they were before. There's no deterioration, so I can continue to follow the proceedings. The doctor's attitude is good. As applies to everybody else at the Detention Unit, I have no complaints, but now that I have this opportunity, I would like, on behalf of myself and my family and friends and everybody else attending the funeral, thank you for your understanding. Nobody expected that I would be allowed to attend, and that had a very positive response among the people. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mrksic. With regard to your state -- one moment. I haven't finished. With regard to your condition of detention, are there any matters you would like to raise? Are you being treated well at the Detention Unit? Any complaints with regard to food or conditions? None. THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation]. No. I have no complaints. I have been a soldier all my life, so these circumstances are quite normal for me except that this is a Detention Unit. Everything else is bearable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mrksic. Colonel Sljivancanin. The same two questions to you. Let's take them one by one. Would you like to raise any matter related to your state of health? THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no health complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And with regard to your conditions of detention? THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Everybody's attitude at the Detention Unit is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is on, but I think he is too tall. That's the problem. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] As I've said, the personnel at the Detention Unit has a proper attitude, and I have no complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Colonel. You may sit down. Finally Mr. Radic. I address the same two questions to you. First, do you -- would you like to raise any matter related to your state of health? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this morning I went to see the doctor taking care of us as I have certain problems with my back. I've asked for some technical assistance. The doctor said that he would look into it. I hope the result would be positive. As far as everything else is concerned, I'm fully satisfied with the treatment given to us at the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is this the first time that you've had this complaint? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] No. I came with that condition. I've simply asked for additional assistance, and the doctor understood this, said that he would look into this, and I hope to receive a reply soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Up until now each time you asked for medical attention and treatment, did you receive it and did you receive it promptly? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Yes. Everything was in order. I'm simply mentioning this because this very morning I asked for certain technical equipment which would facilitate my situation at the Detention Unit. This is the only reason I brought this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Radic. Should you have reason to believe that I should be made aware of further developments in this area, particularly because you are not happy with the situation as it may obtain, I enjoin Mr. Borovic to keep in constant touch with your client -- with his client, and you have every right to draw to my attention anything that is related to your health for which you need or even require or you expect my intervention. So don't be afraid to come forward to me if you need my assistance or need my intervention. THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, I also want to make it clear that I am fully aware of the interest that the administration at the Detention Unit takes in this area. Sometimes it doesn't depend only on the doctor inside the Detention Unit itself. Sometimes the intervention or the help, assistance of the Dutch hospital system is required, too, and I understand that that sometimes takes time. But should there be the need for my intervention, please let me know. THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And with regard to your conditions of detention, Mr. Radic? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Everything is fine for the moment. Thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wish everyone comes forward with that answer. I think that at this point we can adjourn. This Status Conference ends here. The Trial Chamber stands adjourned until the next Status Conference, which will be held within the 120-day limit. As I tried to hint, it may -- probably won't -- as Presiding Judge of Trial Chamber II, I will probably assign this case to another Judge as Pre-Trial Judge, so it may well be that this is the last time you are seeing me here as a Pre-Trial Judge in your case. I will take the decision, because again it has to be a collegial decision more or less, but I will take the decision later on today or in the course of this week. But I can assure you that you will be treated equally if not better. I thank you, and have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Conference adjourned at 5.35 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
